newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia officials differ on U.S. Iraq consultation.
newsitem.headline: Russia officials differ on U.S. Iraq consultation.

text.p: The Russian leadership was not informed of U.S. plans to launch air strikes on Iraq, President Boris Yeltsin's foreign affairs adviser said on Thursday, apparently contradicting an earlier report from Moscow.
"To talk about coordination is simply not serious...The Russian leadership was not informed," Dmitry Ryurikov told a news briefing.
Yeltsin's chief of staff Anatoly Chubais had indicated that Russia had been consulted on Monday, the day before the first wave of strikes, which Moscow has strongly condemned.

"There were consultations with Russia and I recalled that senior foreign ministry officials worked intensively on that problem practically the whole night the day before yesterday and yesterday," Chubais said on Wednesday.
"To raise the question that such a scale of events could have occurred without consultations with Russia is simply irresponsible," he said.

Deputy Foreign Minister Viktor Posuvalyuk came up with yet another version of events surrounding the U.S. strikes against Iraq on Tuesday and Wednesday in retaliation to Baghdad's military operation against separatist Kurds in the north.

"The Russian Federation and the U.S. were in constant contact with one another and the Americans spoke repeatedly about their readiness to take the most diverse measures to alter the situation in northern Iraq," Interfax quoted him as saying.

"We underlined every time that we are categorically opposed to the use of force against Baghdad," he said, adding that judging by President Bill Clinton's remark that the attacks had achieved their goal, he did not expect further strikes.
Russia has described U.S. action as an "inappropriate" raction and demanded that all military actions in the regions are stopped.
Ryurikov said Yeltsin and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl would discuss the events in Iraq when they meet near Moscow on Saturday, although the visit had been arranged before the latest crisis.
"I think that it will not be possible to avoid this issue."

Deputy Foreign Minister Vasily Sidorov said on Thursday Moscow would veto a British draft resolution condemning Iraq for its offensive in the north if it was offered for the United Nations Security Concil unchanged.
The draft condemns Iraq's operations in the northern city of Arbit and "expresses grave concern" about a wider escalation of hostilities in the region. It demands Iraqi troops withdraw immediately.
It makes no mention of the American cruise missiles which blasted Iraqi targets in southern Iraq in response to Baghdad's attacks in the north.

Russia's ambassador to the United Nations Sergei Lavrov had insisted that Baghdad's troops entered their own territory at the request of one Kurdish party and hinted Moscow might abstain if no compromise was found before the draft is put to a vote.
